stories.title: Farah Khan at Edits Film Festival: “Content breakthroughs come from spontaneity, relatability and realness”
stories.summary: Today the curtains came down on the Edits Film Festival in Mumbai, in the presence of filmmaker Farah Khan, festival judges Ahsaas Channa, Dolly Singh, Nikhil Taneja and Rajeev Masand and over 100 content creators in the audience. The post Farah Khan at Edits Film Festival: “Content breakthroughs come from spontaneity, relatability and realness” appeared first on Meta Newsroom .

sources.name: Meta Newsroom
sources.title: Farah Khan at Edits Film Festival: “Content breakthroughs come from spontaneity, relatability and realness”
sources.text: Today the curtains came down on the Edits Film Festival in Mumbai, in the presence of filmmaker Farah Khan, festival judges Ahsaas Channa, Dolly Singh, Nikhil Taneja and Rajeev Masand and over 100 content creators in the audience. The festival awarded its winners – Ishank Gupta ( @filmmaker.ishank ), Sanya Rohillaa ( @bunniestbunnytoeverbunnny ) and Ahsan Vazir ( @ahsan_vazir__ ) for their great storytelling and use of Edits for editing their content. Submissions for the Edits Film Festival commenced in August, where in a duration of 45 days, you were encouraged to submit a piece of content made from unpolished videos in your camera roll, and edited using Edits, Instagram’s video editing app. While the Official Selection played at the festival demonstrated this, the top three in particular, selected by the jury, displayed a rare sense of adventure, restraint and skill. The top three submissions, by Ishank Gupta ( @filmmaker.ishank ), Sanya Rohillaa ( @bunniestbunnytoeverbunnny ) and Ahsan Vazir ( @ahsan_vazir__ ), stood out for diverse storytelling, and use of Edits features in them. The winners were selected by Ahsaas Channa, Dolly Singh, Nikhil Taneja and Rajeev Masand. “Enabling creators with the right tools, platforms and opportunities is central to what we do. The festival opened up new creative possibilities, encouraging creators to experiment with features they hadn’t used before and tell stories in fresh ways. We’re thankful to our jury members and to Farah Khan for the invaluable perspective she shared on her storytelling journey.” – Ankit Rihal, Head of Global Partnerships, Meta, India Film maker Farah Khan was the special guest at the event, who spoke about her approach to content creation and film making, which is a rare combination of someone who’s made feature films for theatres, as well as online content for Reels. “People assume there’s a big plan behind it, but I don’t overthink what I post. Gen Z has inspired me — they’re so nonchalant about it, no second-guessing. Be it a clip from my show, a random chat or a bit of mischief on the spot, everything is spontaneous for me. I think relatability and realness, with a bit of humor, are what audiences actually respond to on Instagram.” – Farah Khan Follow @metaindia and #EditsFilmFestival for seeing more updates from the event.

stories.title: Amp puts AI agents to work beyond code with OpenAI models
stories.summary: See how Amp pushes the frontier of what agents can do with GPT-6 Astra, Ultrafast, GPT-Live-1, and Sign in with ChatGPT.

sources.name: OpenAI
sources.title: Amp puts AI agents to work beyond code with OpenAI models
sources.text: See how Amp pushes the frontier of what agents can do with GPT‑6 Astra, Ultrafast, GPT‑Live‑1, and Sign in with ChatGPT. Amp ⁠ (opens in a new window) is building a frontier AI agent that helps developers turn ambitious ideas into working software. For Quinn Slack, Amp’s CEO, each improvement in the models is an opportunity to expand what the agent can do, from helping developers decide what to build to writing code and designing pages. Amp chooses and recommends models based on what works best for its users, and OpenAI models account for the majority of tokens used in Amp. Quinn shares, “OpenAI is very transparent, and when there are safeguards applied, users know and they understand. That makes it really easy to use OpenAI models. You can do all of your work in Amp with OpenAI models and be really happy.” As builders give agents more work, token costs can become a constraint. Quinn describes some Amp users consuming 10 billion tokens a week. He believes that if people watch every increment of usage, it might hold them back from finding out what an agent is capable of. To help alleviate that, Amp launched its Sign in with ChatGPT integration. Quinn says it gives Amp users access to more tokens and OpenAI models, including GPT‑6 Astra, which changes how willing they are to let an agent take on a larger task. “Sign in with ChatGPT means that people can have that feeling where they’re not counting every single token,” he says. “And once you actually let the agent go and have a longer leash, then you realize just how much it can do.” Quinn says he sees people using the agent to plan, decide what to build, and continue working after they ship. Amp wants agents to help with all the work that goes into building and growing a product. Its own 20-person team uses them that way, including in marketing. “We don’t have someone devoted to it, but we have an agent devoted to it,” Quinn says. The team relies on the agent to improve the experience for new users and help more people discover Amp through search and other channels. For that work, having high-quality writing and design is critical. GPT‑6 Astra helps the team produce documentation and design pages that meet Amp’s exacting standards. Quinn’s experiments with GPT‑6 Astra continue at home. He gave it the plans for his house and used it to create a 3D model in Blender. He and his children then turn that model into games: adding a lazy river through the house or chasing garlic around it, inspired by their grandmother’s dislike of garlic. “And that was not possible just a couple months ago,” he says. Amp recently announced Puck, a conversational AI assistant built into Amp that helps users launch and manage other agents. Users can ask Puck to start an agent to investigate a bug, coordinate several agents, or find a previous conversation about a technical problem. With Calling Puck, powered by GPT‑Live‑1, users can talk to Puck in real time, including from a watch. Quinn imagines people using it to keep their agents working while they’re away from their computers, even while out for a run. Amp has been testing Ultrafast mode with GPT‑6 Astra, and Quinn says the greater speed changes how people use agents. Today, people often switch between several agent tasks while waiting for each to finish. Faster responses could let people juggle fewer agents, or give agents more time to check their own work before returning a result. For Amp, the next step is to bring more of the work before and after coding into the agent, so builders can carry an idea further without handling every step themselves. “There’s this unknown of what humans will create, and that’s what we all get to see. It’s cool to be playing a part in that,” Quinn says.

stories.title: SentinelOne cuts malware analysis from weeks to hours
stories.summary: With OpenAI Daybreak, SentinelOne cuts weeks of malware analysis to hours, creating capacity to investigate more threats.

sources.name: OpenAI
sources.title: SentinelOne cuts malware analysis from weeks to hours
sources.text: With OpenAI Daybreak, SentinelOne cuts weeks of malware analysis to hours, creating capacity to investigate more threats. Hours to reverse-engineer malware, down from 4–6 weeks Reverse engineering a sophisticated piece of malware can take a top security researcher four to six weeks. It’s painstaking work where researchers pull apart software to understand how it behaves, often retracing their steps as they uncover new information. Gregor Stewart, Chief AI Officer at SentinelOne, says OpenAI Daybreak can now produce human-level reverse-engineering output in roughly eight hours. By reducing the time needed for deep analysis, OpenAI gives SentinelOne’s researchers room to investigate more malware and connect findings across samples. That wider view often reveals relationships that isolated investigations might miss. Stewart describes the opportunity as “a kind of intelligence that we were never able to afford before.” Daybreak gives defenders access to OpenAI models for cybersecurity work. SentinelOne uses these capabilities to reverse engineer malware, examining software to understand how it behaves. Faster analysis gives its researchers more capacity to investigate additional samples. Stewart emphasizes that his team remains responsible for the outcome. “The only thing that can’t be automated is accountability,” he says. “Take a decision to change the architecture. This is something that still you would want human eyes on, whereas point fixes or things that don’t fundamentally change the way the software works, those might be better suited for automation,” he adds. Historically, research teams at SentinelOne had to reserve deep investigation for the most interesting or important threats they uncovered. “We were only able to reverse very small numbers of pieces of software,” Stewart says. With fewer samples to compare, they had fewer opportunities to spot connections between threats. Faster analysis with Daybreak gives researchers more opportunities to compare malware samples and look for shared components. For example, a component found in two apparently unrelated samples could give researchers a lead to pursue during a customer investigation. Comparing findings across more samples also reveals broader relationships between threats. Seeing those relationships, Stewart says, “would help you defend further out, and be more proactive about your defense.” Within SentinelOne, Stewart says access to OpenAI’s cyber capabilities is allowing more people to take responsibility for security work. “Almost everyone now has access to the kind of expertise that was in very short supply until maybe even a few months ago,” he says. More team members can investigate issues themselves rather than relying on a small group of specialists. Stewart wants to bring OpenAI’s cyber capabilities into code creation, so SentinelOne developers can address security issues as they build.

stories.title: Crop Regions of Interest & Stitch Them Before VLM Inference
stories.summary: Build a Roboflow Workflow that detects carton damage, crops regions of interest, and stitches them into numbered collages for Gemini inspection. Learn to retain ROI mappings, validate findings, improve crop quality, and compare token costs with separate requests for manufacturing quality inspection.

sources.name: Roboflow
sources.title: Crop Regions of Interest & Stitch Them Before VLM Inference
sources.text: To cut VLM requests without losing detail, use an object detection model to find each region of interest, crop those regions, and stitch them into one numbered collage, so a VLM like Gemini can review up to ten at once and return a finding for each. Roboflow Workflows lets you build this full pipeline (RF-DETR detection, cropping, collage stitching, and structured Gemini reports) in one place, so you can start free and measure the token savings on your own images. Manufacturing quality inspection often comes down to small details. A torn carton edge, a punctured panel, or a crushed corner can reveal packaging damage that needs closer review. An inspection camera captures the whole package, while the evidence needed to assess its condition may occupy only a small part of the image. An object detection model can locate these areas, and a vision-language model (VLM) can describe the visible evidence in each one. As more packages move through inspection, sending every detected region in a separate VLM request repeats the prompt and adds more images to process. Cropping the regions of interest (ROIs) and stitching them into a numbered collage lets the VLM review several areas together while keeping each finding connected to its original location. This tutorial builds that approach in Roboflow Workflows for carton damage inspection. RF-DETR detects potential damage, a custom block packs up to ten crops into each collage page, and Gemini returns structured findings. We will connect the blocks, validate the final report, and explain how to compare token usage and cost with separate crop requests. Crop and stitch ROIs is an image-processing technique that extracts regions of interest from an image and arranges them into a single collage or a series of collage pages. For vision-language model inspection, this groups selected visual evidence into fewer image inputs while preserving a way to connect each finding to its original location. In this tutorial, stitching means assembling separate crops into a collage. Their positions in the collage do not represent their physical arrangement in the original scene. A region of interest, or ROI, is the part of an image selected for further inspection. In this workflow, each ROI comes from a bounding box labeled damage by the detector. Cropping extracts that region from the original image so the VLM can inspect the local evidence. There are two common ways to send this visual evidence to a VLM: Sending the entire image preserves the overall scene, but it also includes the conveyor, background, and package areas that do not need further inspection. Small defects may occupy only a small part of that larger image, making their details harder to assess. Sending multiple crops isolates the areas that need attention. However, sending each crop in a separate request repeats the inspection prompt and requires the model to process another image each time. Multiple crops can also be included in one request, but they remain separate image inputs. Cropping and stitching combines the selected regions into one compact image. Stitching places the crops together in a collage, giving the selected evidence a larger share of the submitted image while reducing the number of image inputs compared with separate crops. For example, ten damage candidates can become one collage containing ten numbered crops. Gemini receives the collage and returns a separate finding for each ROI number, allowing the results to be mapped back to the original detections. The benefit depends on keeping the evidence clear. A crowded collage can make small details difficult to interpret, and tight crops can remove useful context. The later accuracy section explains how to handle crop padding, page size, and ROI mapping. Token savings also need to be measured. One collage is not automatically cheaper than one full-frame image. The often quoted figure of 258 tokens per image comes from a particular tokenization scheme in Google’s image understanding guidance , rather than a universal charge for every Gemini model. Gemini 3 image token usage also depends on media resolution , so compare actual input and output usage when calculating savings. The main processing pattern of the workflow that we will build is detect , crop , stitch , inspect and parse . The complete implementation of the workflow also includes several additional blocks for filtering detections, conditional execution, collecting crops, extracting collage pages, and validating the report. I built an object detection model carton-defect-inspection for this example. The model returns the classes package and damage . In the workflow we will keep only the damage detections, count them, and use that count to control the crop branch. When candidate ROIs are present, their crops are packed into numbered collages and passed to Gemini. Each result remains connected to the original detection through an ROI ID and a stored bounding-box mapping. This makes it possible to review a finding alongside the region that produced it. A separate visualization branch shows the detector's boxes on the original carton image. Try this workflow to view it, run a preview, or fork it into your own workspace. Use the following steps to build the example workflow . Start by creating a Workflow in your Roboflow workspace. Add an image input named image, then add the Project Model block serving your carton detector model endpoint. Name this step model and connect its image input to $inputs.image . The Workflow builder guide explains how to add blocks and connect their inputs and outputs. This project uses the Carton Defect Inspection Model, serving RF-DETR Small . In the supplied definition, the model is referenced through an Inner Workflow . The parent workflow uses its serving configuration, including the detector's confidence threshold. stories.title: How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock
stories.summary: Learn how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock that autonomously investigates and safely remediates cloud security findings from CNAPP and cloud-native sources. The approach drove a 90%+ reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues.

sources.name: AWS Machine Learning
sources.title: How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock
sources.text: Critical cloud exposures pile up faster than security teams can close them. Cloud-native application protection platforms (CNAPP), cloud providers, and posture scanners generate more findings than any team can triage, and risk accumulates in the gap between detected and fixed. Most findings sit untouched, not because they’re hard to fix. Someone must investigate context, identify the owner, confirm the fix won’t break production, and then do it at a volume that outpaces headcount. In this post, we share how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock , to close that gap. Tami autonomously investigates findings ingested from CNAPP and cloud-native sources and assesses whether remediation is safe. It then generates and orchestrates the fix with guardrails and governance wherever a change touches a customer’s cloud. The approach drove an over 90 percent reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues. Tamnoon is an AI-powered cloud security remediation platform that works alongside CNAPPs. Its AI assistant, Tami, helps human cloud security experts investigate, prioritize, and safely remediate misconfigurations and issues across customer environments in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and other cloud providers. Tamnoon integrates with the CNAPPs and cloud-native tools teams already use and turns their findings into validated, production-safe fixes. Most of the work including investigation, prioritization, and remediation planning happens before anything touches a live environment, which is what makes automated remediation trustworthy at scale. A security engineer can spend hours investigating a single finding. Often, it traces back to the same root cause as dozens of other alerts. Tamnoon’s solution addresses the full pipeline from finding ingestion to validated fix. The platform treats these challenges as interconnected rather than isolated problems. Tamnoon takes you from initial finding to executing the fix. The platform ingests findings from CNAPP, Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) providers, and other security tools and normalizes them into a unified schema. It then enriches them with asset and exposure context and prioritizes them. From there, the agentic layer takes over using a set of specialized AI agents, each running in an event-driven, serverless architecture on AWS, so every stage scales independently and fails safely. The platform delegates work to four specialized agents, each responsible for a distinct phase of the remediation pipeline: When the Tamnoon team set out to build Tami, the choice of foundation model (FM) platform was going to shape everything that followed. Tamnoon’s remediation agents don’t all do the same kind of work. Some perform deep investigative reasoning to understand the root cause of a security finding. Others handle high-volume validation, checking proposed fixes quickly and cheaply. Still others review generated code, balancing quality against cost on every task. Matching each of these jobs to the right model, without stitching together a different integration for each one, was a core requirement. That requirement is what made Amazon Bedrock the natural fit. Through a single API, each agent can call the foundation model best suited to its task. The most capable models handle the hardest reasoning. More efficient models take on the repetitive, high-throughput work. Review-focused models optimize the trade-off between output quality and cost. Because it’s one integration rather than many, models can be swapped or upgraded as the landscape evolves, without re-plumbing the architecture each time. Operational overhead at scale was another factor in the decision. As request volume grew, Tamnoon wanted to avoid building and maintaining its own logic to distribute traffic across regional capacity. Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region inference handles this automatically. It automatically routes inference requests to the optimal AWS Region within a defined geographic boundary, maintaining throughput without requiring any custom routing code to operate. Security was the final consideration, and for a cloud security company it was non-negotiable. With Bedrock, inference runs inside Tamnoon’s own AWS environment under AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped permissions. Sensitive customer data never leaves the trust boundary. That gave the team confidence that the platform underpinning Tami met the same standard Tamnoon holds its own service to. Tamnoon sits downstream of the detection tools security teams already run. CNAPPs like Wiz, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Cortex, Upwind, SentinelOne, Orca, and Cyera along with cloud-native services like AWS Security Hub and Amazon GuardDuty are the source of truth for what’s wrong in the environment. Tamnoon connects through API-based integrations and normalizes findings into a common format, so a misconfiguration looks the same whether it came from Wiz or GuardDuty. The detection tools remain the foundation. Tamnoon delivers the end-to-end remediation that follows. For every finding it works, Tami assigns a Remediation Confidence Indicator (RCI) of SAFE, RISKY, or AWAITING DATA. That rating tells teams what can be automated and what needs human review first. Tamnoon runs entirely within its own AWS accounts, isolated per environment. Users access the platform through a single secure entry point built on Amazon API Gateway, with encryption managed by AWS Certificate Manager and sign-in handled by Amazon Cognito. Everything behind that entry point runs in private networks across multiple Availability Zones, so the core platform is never directly exposed to the internet. Inside that environment, Tamnoon combines two kinds of compute. Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) runs the always-on services behind the dashboard, while AWS Lambda powers the event-driven work of collecting findings, analyzing them, and executing remediations. stories.title: Generate presentations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
stories.summary: This post walks you through building an AI agent system with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates PowerPoint presentation creation from enterprise documents. A supervisor agent, Retrieval Augmented Generation, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails generate grounded presentations in under 90 seconds.

sources.name: AWS Machine Learning
sources.title: Generate presentations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
sources.text: A financial services team spends significant time each week manually creating client PowerPoint presentations from quarterly reports, compliance documents, and market analyses. Each presentation requires reading hundreds of pages, extracting key data points, structuring slides, and generating supporting visuals. This post walks you through building an AI agent system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates this workflow, completing in under 90 seconds in our internal testing. This approach reduces presentation creation time while grounding content in source documents. The solution deploys a supervisor agent on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, using the Strands Agents framework to orchestrate document generation and summarization tools. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (available on Amazon Bedrock) handles content creation, Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2 powers vector search, and Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint (available on Amazon Bedrock) generates slide images. This post includes a public repository with the code assets. The solution deploys a single supervisor agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime that selects between document generation and summarization tools based on user requests. A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline uses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for vector storage and semantic search across multimodal content. The solution includes a REST API built with .NET 8 minimal APIs, so you can integrate with existing enterprise applications through standard HTTP calls. AWS Lambda offers serverless compute, including containerized functions for PowerPoint generation. The solution secures the implementation with Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) isolation, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) least-privilege access control. This section covers AgentCore runtime, RAG, and content safety guardrails as they apply to this solution. A single AI agent generating documents from large knowledge bases must retrieve content, structure outlines, generate text, create images, and assemble files. Rather than implementing these competing responsibilities in a monolithic function, the solution uses a tool-based architecture where a supervisor agent routes requests to specialized tools. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime provides a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent code runs in an isolated container with session management, built-in identity, and observability. The solution uses the Strands Agents framework (an open source SDK for building AI agents) to implement the supervisor logic. The agent determines whether a request requires document generation, content summarization, or both, then invokes the appropriate tool. You can add new capabilities by defining new tools in the agent code without modifying existing ones. RAG addresses a fundamental challenge in AI systems: delivering accurate, up-to-date information grounded in enterprise data rather than relying solely on the model’s training data. The implementation uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases , which combine vector search with large language models (LLMs) to retrieve relevant context before generating responses. This approach is designed to help reduce hallucinated content by grounding generated documents in source information from the enterprise knowledge base. Note: The Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection data plane must remain publicly accessible because Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases accesses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless from AWS-managed infrastructure, not through customer VPC endpoints. IAM data access policies protect the collection, and VPC-only access restricts the Amazon OpenSearch Serverless dashboard. Enterprise AI applications require content moderation to meet organizational standards and compliance requirements. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails offers built-in content filtering and safety mechanisms integrated throughout the document generation pipeline. The implementation creates custom guardrails through AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) , configured with specific policies tailored to enterprise document creation. The agent applies guardrails at the model invocation level, providing consistent content safety without requiring manual configuration for each deployment. The following diagram illustrates the agent-based document generation system. Figure 1: Architecture of the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore RAG presentation generation system The data flow begins with user requests arriving through Amazon API Gateway , which routes them to a .NET-based Chat API running on AWS Lambda . The API maintains conversation state in Amazon DynamoDB . It then invokes the supervisor agent hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime. The supervisor agent analyzes the request and selects the appropriate tool. For document generation, it invokes the PPTX Generator Lambda (a containerized Python function). For summarization, the supervisor invokes the Summary Generator Lambda, which queries the knowledge base through the retrieve_and_generate API. The system processes, chunks, and embeds documents stored in Amazon S3 using Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2. Amazon OpenSearch Serverless indexes the embeddings for fast semantic search. When tools query the knowledge base, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless retrieves relevant chunks, which are then supplied as context to Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (on Amazon Bedrock) for generating grounded responses. The system stores generated documents in Amazon S3 and returns presigned URLs for secure download. sources.title: Building trust in AI agents: A production-ready evaluation framework with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
sources.text: Every organization racing to deploy AI agents faces the same reckoning: an agent that demos beautifully can quietly degrade in production, and by the time a human notices, the trust is already broken. Where traditional software fails loudly, agents fail softly. They return an answer that looks confident, reads fluently, and is wrong. When that answer drives a real business decision, the cost is not a broken feature. It’s a broken relationship with the user. That’s the quality problem at its core. The challenge is therefore not building agents that work once, but proving they keep working, at scale, across every sub-agent, every workflow, and every release. The teams that win the agent era will be the ones who treat quality not as a final QA step but as the operating system of the agent itself: continuously measured, automatically defended, and improved with every interaction. In this post, we show how we built a continuous quality loop for production-ready agentic solutions at scale using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The solution uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and other AWS services for internal use, so sellers and sales leaders can ask business questions in plain English from Amazon Quick. Behind that single experience, several specialized sub-agents work together: the Performance Insights Agent for territory-scoped revenue and performance, the Customer Insights Agent for customer intelligence, the Data Insights Agent for text-to-SQL over foundational datasets, and direct dashboard access. Answers are scoped to each user’s territory and role-level security. Field teams use these answers to assist in planning account strategy, prepare for customer meetings, so the numbers must be right. The most damaging failure is not a crash. It’s a fluent, confident answer that is quietly wrong. Before launch, when we evaluated the Customer Insights Agent, we found exactly that: Through the different runs, monitoring stayed green. It told us the system had responded, not whether the answer was right. Had these errors shipped uncaught, the field would have paid for them. A seller who repeats an inflated figure can lose credibility with the customer. This is exactly why we caught it before launch. The risk doesn’t end at launch: it grows with every new agent and every change to data, prompts, code, or models. It also grows without any release, because upstream pipelines refresh the data every week. Coordinated releases introduce a related risk: when a data change, a tool change, and a paired prompt update are meant to ship together but land apart, the system runs mismatched until all changes catch up. In one pre-production test, that mismatch window by itself dropped the pass rate from 78 percent to 38 percent. To catch failures like these, before every release and continuously in production, we need a framework that can show whether answers are grounded and correct, and trace each failure back to its root cause in the data, the prompt, or the agent’s code. At AWS, the Sales, Marketing, and Global Services (SMGS) Operations team developed a production multi-agent system serving AWS Field Sales worldwide. It serves two distinct audiences. For field sales teams, it replaces hours of manual data analysis with on-demand, conversational intelligence, helping sellers understand the health of their business, surface risks and opportunities, and take action faster. For leadership, it powers business management cadences including Weekly Business Reviews (WBRs), surfacing the signals that matter across the portfolio without requiring manual report preparation. The same agentic system serves both the seller on the front line and the leader reviewing performance at scale. The agentic system orchestrates a growing portfolio of specialized sub-agents, each owning a distinct capability domain. Among them: the Performance Insights Agent generates natural-language business intelligence narratives from complex sales data, turning raw metrics into actionable seller insights. The Customer Insights Agent assembles a 360-degree view of each customer by synthesizing signals across product usage, support history, contract status, and engagement data, helping sellers understand where a customer is in their journey and what they need next. The Data Insights Agent is a text-to-SQL agent that account teams use to query structured analytics data in plain English without writing a single line of SQL. These three agents are the ones referenced throughout the rest of this post. Coordinating these agents reliably at scale made one thing clear: agentic quality wasn’t an operational concern to manage later. It was the prerequisite for operating. A single degraded sub-agent can silently corrupt every response downstream, and traditional monitoring won’t catch it. That reality made a full lifecycle evaluation framework not optional but necessary. AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is the connective tissue powering it, alongside Amazon Bedrock Guardrails (safety), Amazon CloudWatch (metrics, alarms, tracing), Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and Amazon Redshift (evaluation persistence), Amazon Quick (dashboards), and AWS Lambda (custom evaluators). In this post, we share how we tackled the hardest operational challenges in running AI agents at enterprise scale, and how Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations became the backbone of agent quality. Specifically, we cover: Traditional software is deterministic: the same input produces the same output. Machine learning (ML) models introduced probabilistic outputs, and MLOps emerged to manage their training, versioning, monitoring, and re-training. AI agents add a third layer of operational complexity: autonomous, multi-step reasoning, where the question shifts from “did something break?” to “is the agent making sound decisions across its entire reasoning chain?” Agents inherit the hard problems of both predecessors, and introduce some new ones.
